schools.name: Dubstep
schools.description: Dubstep is sparse, dark electronic music built on syncopated rhythms and huge sub-bass, almost always around 140 beats per minute. It emerged in South London in the early 2000s as an offshoot of UK garage, blending 2-step rhythms with dub's spacious production and touches of drum and bass and grime. A harsher American offshoot, brostep, later made it a US festival sound.
schools.debatable: The name has more than one claimed origin (Neil Jolliffe of Tempa is said to have coined it in 2002, but 'dub step' was in use by 2001), and some use 'brostep' as a put-down for the louder American style.
schools.tagline: Dark, spacious South London bass music at 140 bpm, born from UK garage.
questions: A clap or snare usually on the third beat of each bar at about 140 bpm, with tracks so empty that, as Kode9 put it, you 'almost fill in the double time yourself'.
Prominent sub-bass and, in some strands, the 'wobble': a long bass note made to pulse rhythmically.
Lots of empty space and minor keys, with the bass dropping in hard after a pause.

themes.name: Big Apple and FWD>>
themes.text: Croydon's Big Apple record shop and the FWD>> club night, founded in 2001 and later held at Plastic People, were where the sound took shape. Skream worked in the shop as a teenager and Benga was a regular there.

themes.name: Sound-system thinking
themes.text: Digital Mystikz (Mala and Coki), with Loefah and MC Sgt Pokes, brought sound-system thinking, dub values and jungle's bass weight, and DMZ fliers told dancers to 'come meditate on bass weight'. A 600-person queue at the DMZ night's first anniversary in Brixton is seen as a pivotal moment.

themes.name: Radio takes it worldwide
themes.text: John Peel played dubstep from 2003, and Mary Anne Hobbs's 2006 'Dubstep Warz' show on BBC Radio 1 gave a UK underground scene a global audience.

themes.name: Melody and ghosts
themes.text: Skream's 'Midnight Request Line' (2005) pushed dubstep towards melody and crossed over. Burial's albums, full of vinyl crackle, rain and pitch-shifted voices, took its dark mood somewhere emotional and haunted.

themes.name: Brostep and after
themes.text: Around 2010–11 dubstep reached the pop charts, and in the US a harsher, metal-edged style called brostep made it a mass sound, swapping deep sub-bass for mid-range riffs. Some UK pioneers moved on: Skream to house and techno, Loefah to UK bass.

schools.name: EDM (2010s boom)
schools.description: 'EDM', short for electronic dance music, is an old umbrella name that the American music industry pushed in the late 2000s and early 2010s to rebrand US rave culture. The boom it labelled was a big-stage, drop-heavy sound somewhere between electro and progressive house, played by celebrity DJs at festivals such as Electric Daisy Carnival and Ultra. It made dance music central to US pop until the boom levelled off in the late 2010s.
schools.debatable: Is it a genre at all? The industry treated 'EDM' as a brand, but the name is still used as an umbrella for many older genres, and in the UK people tend to just say 'dance music'.
schools.tagline: The 2010s US festival boom of drop-heavy, stadium-sized dance music.
questions: A long build that pauses, then explodes into 'the drop', made for festival crowds.
Big electro and progressive house synths at around 128 beats per minute, often with pop vocals on top.
In its dubstep-influenced strand, harsh 'brostep' bass riffs compared to heavy metal.

themes.name: A rebrand for rave
themes.text: Electronic dance music was already a wide family of genres when, by the early 2010s, the US industry and music press began pushing 'EDM' as a fresh label for American rave culture, setting it apart from 1990s raves.

themes.name: Pop crossovers
themes.text: From 2009 David Guetta scored regular crossover hits with pop and hip-hop stars, such as 'When Love Takes Over' with Kelly Rowland. Avicii later blended house with folk and country on 'Wake Me Up'.

themes.name: Festivals and stadiums
themes.text: Festivals such as Electric Daisy Carnival and Ultra grew huge, with DJs as celebrities and big visual shows. In December 2011 Swedish House Mafia became the first electronic act to sell out New York's Madison Square Garden.

themes.name: The brostep strand
themes.text: Skrillex popularised a harsher dubstep sound called brostep, compared to heavy metal in its aggression. In 2011 Spin hailed a 'new rave generation' led by Guetta, Deadmau5 and Skrillex.

themes.name: Big business, and backlash
themes.text: From 2012 corporations bought up festivals and promoters, and brands used EDM to reach young people. Veteran DJs criticised 'press-play' sets, Deadmau5 said popular EDM 'all sounds the same', Avicii said most of it lacked longevity, and by the late 2010s the boom had plateaued.

schools.name: Traditional pop (with Tin Pan Alley)
schools.description: Traditional pop is the Western popular music that generally came before rock and roll and pop in the mid-1950s, built on songs by Broadway, Hollywood and Tin Pan Alley songwriters; Tin Pan Alley's publishers go back to about 1885. Many of the songs became 'standards', so widely known that many artists recorded them, and the swing era made stars of singers such as Bing Crosby, Frank Sinatra and Patti Page. Since the 1980s, rock and pop stars such as Linda Ronstadt have revived the standards on hit albums.
schools.debatable: Where it starts and stops is fuzzy: Tin Pan Alley is usually dated from about 1885, but some end it with the Depression in the 1930s and others with rock and roll in the 1950s.
schools.tagline: The songwriters' and crooners' pop of the Great American Songbook, before rock and roll.
questions: A singer out front, with lush string sections and full orchestral arrangements behind the voice.
Close, conversational microphone singing (crooning) instead of belting to the back row.
Simple, direct words and melodies written to be sung by anyone, from a star to an amateur at the piano.

themes.name: Songs as sheet music
themes.text: Tin Pan Alley is usually dated from about 1885, when music publishers set up shop in one Manhattan district, originally a stretch of West 28th Street. Families bought sheet music to play new songs at home, and 'song pluggers' at the piano demonstrated new tunes to push sales. The name probably mocks the din of many cheap pianos playing at once, and Irving Berlin was among the writers who frequented it.

sources.section: New York City before Tin Pan Alley

themes.name: Writers behind the songs
themes.text: The music was built by professional songwriters for Broadway, Hollywood and the publishers. Irving Berlin, who arrived from Russia as a child, wrote around 1,500 songs in plain, everyday language, and many Jewish immigrants worked as publishers and songwriters on Tin Pan Alley.

themes.name: Ragtime, jazz and blues
themes.text: Tin Pan Alley started with melodramatic ballads and comic novelty songs, then took up the cakewalk (a strutting dance rhythm) and ragtime, and in the 1910s and 1920s published songs in the new jazz and blues styles, though less completely, since its songs had to suit amateur singers. Writers note an African American influence from ragtime, the blues and jazz. Berlin's 'Alexander's Ragtime Band' (1911) revived the ragtime craze.

themes.name: The microphone voice
themes.text: Recording microphones let singers drop the loud vaudeville style. Bing Crosby sang with an intimate, conversational ease that earned the name 'crooner' and influenced many male singers after him, Frank Sinatra among them.

themes.name: Strings and the album
themes.text: From the mid-1940s, string sections, orchestral arrangements and more focus on the vocal defined the sound. In the 1950s the long-playing record let Sinatra and arranger Nelson Riddle build whole moody albums around one theme, while Patti Page leaned her hits toward country.

schools.name: Pop music
schools.description: Pop took its modern form in the US and UK in the mid-1950s; at first the word covered rock and roll and the youth styles it inspired. From the late 1960s pop came to mean the more commercial, accessible side of popular music: songs of about three minutes with a hook-filled chorus and a beat you can dance to. It keeps borrowing from other styles, from rock and country to hip-hop and dance music.
schools.debatable: Pop is hard to pin down: some define it by sound, others simply as whatever becomes popular, and it is often set against rock as 'singles for teenagers' versus 'albums for adults'.
schools.tagline: Short, catchy, chorus-led songs made to reach everyone, from the 1950s to now.
questions: A verse that builds to a chorus designed to stick in your ear through simple repetition.
Short songs, usually two and a half to three and a half minutes, with a clear, steady beat you can dance to.
Polished studio production, from 1960s echo and strings to 1980s synthesizers and today's electronic dance beats.

themes.name: Out of rock and roll
themes.text: In the mid-1950s 'pop music' was a British name for rock and roll and the youth styles around it, and early pop also drew on traditional pop. Only from about 1967 did pop and rock start to mean different things.

themes.name: Built in the studio
themes.text: Pop leans on recording and production more than live playing. Better microphones, the 45 rpm single, multi-track recording and later digital sampling all changed how it was made, and 1960s producers such as Phil Spector built huge echoing sounds.

themes.name: Made for the screen
themes.text: Television made pop stars need a visual presence, and in the early 1980s MTV favoured artists with strong visual appeal. Michael Jackson's 'Thriller' video helped break racial barriers on the channel, and Madonna used the music video to shape her songs and her image.

themes.name: Global superstars
themes.text: In the late 20th century a handful of pop singers became global superstars, among them Whitney Houston, Michael Jackson, Madonna, George Michael and Prince. Houston brought a gospel-trained voice into chart pop.

themes.name: Club beats take over
themes.text: Around 2000 the Swedish 'Cheiron sound' partly shaped the pop of Britney Spears, the Backstreet Boys and NSYNC. Her 2007 album Blackout mixed EDM, R&B and hip-hop, and by 2010 dance-influenced pop ruled the charts, with clubs rather than radio setting trends.

schools.name: K-pop
schools.description: K-pop grew in South Korea in the 1990s as a youth subculture, with Korean musicians drawing on Western dance music, hip-hop, R&B and rock. Today the name mostly means the music of teen idol acts, chiefly girl groups and boy bands, who emphasise visual appeal and performance. It is known for its melodies and its blend of styles, and in the 2010s social media and the Korean Wave (the global spread of South Korean pop culture) carried it around the world.
schools.debatable: How Korean K-pop really is gets argued over, as more songs are written by Western songwriters, sung in English and aimed at a global audience; some call it a new 'transnational' culture.
schools.tagline: South Korea's idol pop: hybrid songs, sharp group dances and bold visuals.
questions: Several styles in one song, often pop, hip-hop, R&B and electronic music, with rap verses next to big sung choruses.
English phrases mixed into Korean lyrics, song titles and group names.
A 'point' dance: a short, hooky, repeated move in the choreography, tied to the song's lyrics.

themes.name: Rap dance arrives
themes.text: In 1992 Seo Taiji and Boys debuted with 'I Know', a mix of new jack swing beats (which combine hip-hop and soul), rap verses, pop choruses and new dance moves that scored lowest with the TV jury but became a huge hit. Their fusion of hip-hop, techno and rock is often traced as K-pop's starting point.

themes.name: The idol system
themes.text: The band's success with teenagers turned the industry toward teen pop. Lee Soo-man of SM Entertainment developed the Korean idol system, adapting a trainee model from Japan's idol industry: young recruits train for years in singing, dancing, languages and media skills before a debut. H.O.T. (1996) was one of the first idol boy bands.

themes.name: Dance as the core
themes.text: Dance is central: members swap places in quick, synchronised 'formation changes', and routines centre on a repeated 'point' move tied to the lyrics. Seo Taiji and Boys were the first to make dance, including breakdancing, the main feature of a performance.

themes.name: The Korean Wave
themes.text: By the early 2000s BoA and TVXQ were successful in Japan, and H.O.T. had already found fans in China and Taiwan. In the 2010s the Korean Wave and social media made acts like BTS and Blackpink international stars.

themes.name: Control and its costs
themes.text: K-pop is known for tight management, and four companies dominate it: SM, YG, JYP and Hybe. The training system and the industry's commercialism and treatment of artists are often criticised, though the 2020s have brought more artist autonomy.

schools.name: Indie rock
schools.description: Indie rock grew in the UK, the US and New Zealand in the early-to-mid 1980s, out of punk's do-it-yourself idea that anyone could make and release a record. The name first meant rock put out on small, low-budget independent labels; by the 1990s it described the sound such bands made. It covers a wide range, tied together more by an attitude of independence from mainstream tastes than by one sound.
schools.debatable: Its edge with alternative rock is blurry: in the US the two were long treated as the same thing, and after Nirvana's breakthrough 'indie' turned from a label status into a style, even a marketing tag.
schools.tagline: Guitar rock with a do-it-yourself spirit, first named for its small independent labels.
questions: Jangly or noisy guitars, often in small guitar-band line-ups, drawing on punk and 1960s pop and rock.
Rough, low-budget 'lo-fi' recording that makes the do-it-yourself approach part of the sound.
In bands like Pavement, 'fractured' song structures, squalls of feedback and humorous, often sarcastic lyrics.

themes.name: Make your own record
themes.text: On 29 January 1977 Manchester's Buzzcocks put out the four-track Spiral Scratch EP on their own label, a moment the BBC calls pivotal for indie. Its sleeve showed how the record was made, and a wave of bands started pressing and distributing their own records.

themes.name: From Dunedin to college radio
themes.text: New Zealand's Dunedin sound, from bands on Flying Nun Records such as the Chills and the Clean, shaped indie's sound. In the US, college radio played jangle pop bands (named for their jangly guitars) like R.E.M. and the Smiths, and 'college rock' was later renamed 'indie'.

themes.name: The underground solidifies
themes.text: In the mid-1980s the NME's C86 cassette gathered Britain's indie scene, and in the US Sonic Youth's underground success helped define the genre. Sonic Youth came out of New York's experimental no wave scene and pushed noise and strange guitar tunings into rock.

themes.name: Women at the front
themes.text: Indie rock has more women artists than earlier rock styles, most visibly in feminist riot grrrl bands such as Bikini Kill. The band urged women to come to the front at shows, though women running indie labels stayed rare.

themes.name: Split, then revival
themes.text: After grunge broke into the mainstream, indie split into radio-friendly bands and experimental ones; Pavement's lo-fi Slanted and Enchanted (1992) came to stand for the underground side. In 2001 the Strokes' Is This It brought indie back into the mainstream through the garage rock and post-punk revival.

reactedAgainst.text: In the 1990s indie rock defined itself against alternative rock once it went mainstream after Nirvana: it was made by artists who could not or would not cross over, and who were wary of alternative rock's 'macho' style.

schools.name: Post-punk (with new wave)
schools.description: Post-punk grew in the late 1970s, mainly in Britain, as bands kept punk's do-it-yourself energy but dropped its raw simplicity for a more experimental approach. They borrowed from dub (reggae remixed by stripping and reworking existing recordings), funk, disco, krautrock (experimental German rock), electronics and avant-garde art, and from writers such as J. G. Ballard and William S. Burroughs. Its lighter, more pop-oriented relative, new wave, grew up alongside it, reached the charts from late 1978 and spread across America through MTV; both have had revivals since the 2000s.
schools.debatable: The label has no agreed definition: it names both a sound and a period (roughly 1978–84), several defining bands existed before punk broke, and 'post-punk' and 'new wave' were at first used interchangeably.
schools.tagline: Punk's experimental aftermath: melodic bass, angular guitars, dub and art-school ideas.
questions: Melodic basslines that carry the tune, leaving the guitars free to add angular stabs and atmosphere.
Dub-style space and echo, funk and disco rhythms, and steady, insistent drumming.
Spoken or detached vocals; in new wave, choppy guitars, synthesizers and a quirky, jittery pop feel.

themes.name: Punk, broken open
themes.text: By late 1977 some British bands felt punk had become a formula and a parody of itself. Siouxsie and the Banshees, Wire and the Slits began experimenting, and in 1978 John Lydon left the Sex Pistols to form Public Image Ltd, seeking an 'anti-rock' project.

themes.name: Dub, funk and disco
themes.text: Post-punk swapped rock-and-roll riffs for non-rock styles. PiL built an abrasive, bass-heavy sound from dub, noise and disco, while Leeds art students Gang of Four played a stripped-down mix of punk, funk and dub with political lyrics.

themes.name: Space in the studio
themes.text: Producers such as Martin Hannett, Steve Lillywhite and Dennis Bovell devised unorthodox studio techniques. Hannett gave Joy Division an eerie sense of space, with Peter Hook's bass carrying the melody and the guitar leaving gaps, on records for Manchester's independent Factory label.

themes.name: Into the dark
themes.text: By 1979 gothic rock grew out of the scene, pioneered by bands with darker subject matter such as Siouxsie and the Banshees and Joy Division. Bleak, deindustrialising cities in Britain, and the industrial landscapes around the New York and Ohio scenes, shaped much of this mood.

themes.name: New wave's pop side
themes.text: New wave took a lighter, more melodic route, with hooks, quirky humour and synths. Sire Records' Seymour Stein pushed the name to sell his acts from CBGB, the New York punk club; Blondie, from the same scene, had 'Heart of Glass', the first new wave single to reach number one in the US, and MTV spread new wave across America from 1981.

reactedAgainst.text: Post-punk bands took punk's energy and DIY spirit but rejected what punk had become by 1977: a commercial formula of raw, simple, three-chord rock.

schools.name: Krautrock
schools.description: Krautrock is a broad family of experimental rock that grew in West Germany in the late 1960s and early 1970s. Bands mixed psychedelic rock, avant-garde composition and early electronic music, and swapped rock's blues roots and verse-chorus songs for hypnotic rhythms, long improvisations and tape experiments. The scene helped shape ambient music and techno and fed into post-punk; newer bands still play in its style.
schools.debatable: The name itself: 'krautrock' was popularised by the British music press as a mocking umbrella label, many of the musicians disliked it, and some preferred 'kosmische Musik' (cosmic music).
schools.tagline: West Germany's hypnotic experimental rock, built on long grooves and early synths.
questions: The motorik beat: a steady, kick-drum-heavy 4/4 pulse that feels like it is always rolling forward.
Long stretches of repetition, drone and texture instead of verses and choruses.
Early synthesizers and tape tricks (musique concrète: music built from recorded sounds that are cut, spliced and reshaped).

themes.name: A break with the past
themes.text: Krautrock grew partly out of the 1968 student protests. Young West Germans wanted a popular music of their own, free of the country's Nazi past, of American dominance and of conservative German entertainment such as schlager pop.

themes.name: The motorik beat
themes.text: A common thread is the motorik beat, a pulsing, kick-drum-heavy 4/4 groove. Neu!'s Klaus Dinger and Can's Jaki Liebezeit are credited with pioneering it; Can used it in 'Mother Sky', Neu! probably first on their debut album, and Kraftwerk in 'Autobahn'.

themes.name: Avant-garde schooling
themes.text: Some players came from serious music and jazz rather than rock. Can's Holger Czukay and Irmin Schmidt had studied with the composer Karlheinz Stockhausen, and the scene also drew on minimalists, free jazz and Miles Davis's In a Silent Way.

themes.name: Cut, splice, collage
themes.text: Tape was an instrument. Can edited long improvisations into albums, Faust built The Faust Tapes from spliced private recordings, and Neu! filled half of Neu! 2 with sped-up and slowed-down versions of their own single, one of the earliest remixes.

themes.name: Towards the machines
themes.text: A more electronic strand, often called kosmische Musik, used synthesizers for spacey, often instrumental soundscapes. Kraftwerk began in the krautrock scene and moved to synthesizers, drum machines and vocoders, and the wider scene led directly to the Düsseldorf and Berlin schools of electronic music.

schools.name: Dancehall
schools.description: Dancehall is Jamaican popular music that began in the late 1970s as a sparer offshoot of roots reggae, named after the dance halls where sound systems played. It grew among working-class people in inner-city Kingston, with deejays toasting (chanting and talking rhythmically) in Jamaican Patois over instrumentals called riddims. In the mid-1980s it went digital and faster, and from the 2000s it reached the global pop charts.
schools.debatable: Whether it is reggae at all: dancehall's gold chains and gritty lyrics were far from roots reggae, and purists argued over whether it should count as an extension of reggae.
schools.tagline: Kingston's sound-system music: deejays chanting in Patois over shared riddims.
questions: A deejay toasting (half chanting, half talking) in Jamaican Patois rather than standard English.
A riddim: one instrumental track that many different singers voice, so you may hear the same beat under several songs.
Sparse, digital rhythms from electronic keyboards and drum machines, faster than 1970s roots reggae.

themes.name: Sound systems, not radio
themes.text: Conservative Jamaican radio would not play the music, so it spread through sound systems: huge mobile speaker rigs set up in open-air venues in Kingston's inner city. Sound-system operators, deejays and selectors became performers in their own right, and Yellowman learned his craft at sound-system dances.

themes.name: A new generation of deejays
themes.text: In the early 1980s a new wave of deejays took over from the older toasters. Yellowman became the first Jamaican deejay signed to a major American label, and women deejays such as Lady G and Sister Nancy emerged, with Lady Saw following later in the decade.

themes.name: Going digital
themes.text: In 1985 Wayne Smith's 'Under Me Sleng Teng', produced by King Jammy, used a rhythm from a digital keyboard and was reused on over 200 records. Digital riddims became the norm; Shabba Ranks's 'Dem Bow' riddim later became the backbone of reggaeton.

themes.name: Slackness and controversy
themes.text: Many hits dealt frankly with sex, a style called slackness; Lady Saw's shows were banned in parts of Jamaica while equally lewd male shows were not. The genre has also been criticised for violent and anti-gay lyrics, which in some cases led to cancelled concerts and to campaigns such as Stop Murder Music; many artists have since apologised.

themes.name: From Kingston to the charts
themes.text: Shabba Ranks won back-to-back Grammy awards in the early 1990s, and Sean Paul's 'Get Busy' (2003) became the first dancehall single to top the US Billboard Hot 100. In the 2010s dancehall-flavoured hits by Rihanna and Drake carried its rhythms further.

schools.name: Son cubano (with mambo)
schools.description: Son cubano is a Cuban music and dance that grew in the eastern highlands in the late 19th century, blending a Spanish-derived guitar, the tres, and song style with clave rhythm, call and response and percussion of Bantu origin. It reached Havana around 1909, was first recorded in 1917 and became Cuba's most popular genre, growing from small groups into sextets, septets and conjuntos. Mambo grew out of the danzón using son's repeating figures, and son is considered the foundation of salsa.
schools.debatable: Where it began: historically most musicologists pointed to rural eastern Cuba, but versions of son appeared across rural Cuba by the 1890s, Peter Manuel argues much of its structure came from the Havana contradanza, and the old 'Ma Teodora' origin story is generally considered apocryphal.
schools.tagline: Cuba's Spanish-African song behind salsa; mambo grew from the danzón with son's figures.
questions: The tres (a small Cuban guitar) playing a guajeo, a short repeating figure (ostinato) that recurs across many son songs.
The clave, a five-note rhythmic 'key' pattern that the whole song is built around, plus bongos and maracas.
Call and response: a lead singer improvising against a repeated chorus, especially in the closing montuno section.

themes.name: Spanish and Bantu roots
themes.text: Son mixes Spanish elements (the vocal style, verse metre and the tres, derived from the Spanish guitar) with clave, call and response and percussion rooted in Bantu traditions. Its early forms, like changüí and nengón, were made by eastern peasants, many of Bantu origin.

themes.name: Coming to Havana
themes.text: Around 1909 son reached Havana, where formerly enslaved people and rural migrants met and rumba traditions mixed. The first documented son recording was made in 1917, and in 1918 María Teresa Vera sang lead and played clave for the Sexteto Habanero Godínez.

themes.name: The sextet era
themes.text: In the 1920s the sextet of guitar, tres, bongos, claves, maracas and double bass became the classic format, and trumpets soon made septets. Radio from 1922 helped turn son into perhaps Cuba's most popular music, Vera led the Sexteto Occidente, and the Trío Matamoros carried son across Latin America.

themes.name: Arsenio's conjunto
themes.text: In 1940 Arsenio Rodríguez formed one of the first conjuntos, adding more trumpets, piano and conga drums to the son line-up, though others had tried these elements before. His layered guajeos and clave-tight son montuno became the template for salsa.

themes.name: Mambo and after
themes.text: Mambo began in the late 1930s with Arcaño y sus Maravillas, whose López brothers named a final improvised section of the danzón, built on son's guajeos, a 'mambo'. Pérez Prado made it a brass-heavy big-band craze from Mexico City; later son lived on in salsa, timba and the Buena Vista Social Club revival.

schools.name: Samba
schools.description: Samba is a broad name for Brazilian rhythms that grew in Afro-Brazilian communities of Bahia in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, with roots in West African traditions. In Rio de Janeiro it became a song genre with 'Pelo Telefone' (1917), and in the late 1920s the sambistas of the Estácio neighbourhood gave it the faster, drum-heavy, syncopated form that is today synonymous with samba. Once criminalised, it became a symbol of Brazil and branched into bossa nova, pagode and many other styles.
schools.debatable: Its first record: 'Pelo Telefone' is often called the first samba, but some scholars note earlier songs labelled samba, its rhythm and instruments were closer to maxixe, and Donga's sole authorship was soon contested by some of his contemporaries.
schools.tagline: Brazil's Afro-Brazilian drum-and-chorus music, born in Bahia and remade in Rio.
questions: A batucada (samba's percussion groove) in a two-beat (2/4) feel, with the deep surdo drum marking the pulse under pandeiro, tamborim and cuíca.
A sung chorus that returns between verses; Estácio-style sambas are organised in a first and a second part.
Classical guitar and the cavaquinho (a small four-string guitar) filling in the harmony around the drums.

themes.name: Little Africa in Rio
themes.text: After abolition, many Black Bahians moved to Rio and formed a community called 'Little Africa'. Bahian women known as the Tias Baianas hosted religious and musical gatherings; at Tia Ciata's house musicians such as Donga, Pixinguinha and João da Baiana played together.

themes.name: Pelo Telefone
themes.text: In 1916 Donga registered 'Pelo Telefone' as a 'carnival samba', and Baiano's recording was a huge hit at the 1917 Carnival. It marked the official start of samba as a song genre, though its 'first' status and its authorship are both disputed.

themes.name: The Estácio sound
themes.text: In the late 1920s sambistas from Rio's Estácio neighbourhood, Ismael Silva among them, made samba faster and more syncopated for street parades, with the surdo driving it. To avoid police harassment they organised samba schools; Cartola helped found Mangueira in 1928.

sources.section: Samba do Estácio, the genesis of urban samba

themes.name: Radio and record stars
themes.text: In the 1930s radio made samba national. Noel Rosa, from middle-class Vila Isabel, helped make Estácio samba respectable, and Carmen Miranda was the first artist to promote samba abroad. White performers were favoured, while poor Black sambistas were often left as suppliers of songs.

sources.section: Radio era and popularization of samba

themes.name: From crime to heritage
themes.text: Early samba was criminalised: gatherings were broken up and instruments destroyed, an attitude rooted in racism, classism and religious intolerance. By the 1960s traditional samba was being championed as 'resistance music' at places like Cartola and Dona Zica's bar Zicartola, and in 2007 Carioca samba was declared Brazilian cultural heritage.

schools.name: Highlife
schools.description: Highlife is Ghanaian music that grew in the coastal towns of the Gold Coast in the 19th century, through colonial rule and trade. It lays Western jazz melodies and instruments over local African rhythms, led by jazzy horns and two-finger-picked guitars. It spread across West Africa, became Igbo highlife in 1960s Nigeria, and lives on in gospel highlife and a newer synth-driven sound.
schools.debatable: When it began: its roots are dated to the 1870s Gold Coast, but the name 'highlife' only appeared in the early 1920s, and Jacob Asare's 1928 recordings are credited as the first in the genre.
schools.tagline: Ghana's guitar-and-horn dance music, a root of both Afrobeat and afrobeats.
questions: Jazzy horns and guitars leading the band over local African rhythms.
Two-finger guitar picking, which highlife guitarists built from the dagomba style borrowed from Liberian Kru sailors.
A bell pattern that Cubans call the clave; it is indigenous to Ghana and used in highlife.

themes.name: Palm-wine roots
themes.text: One root was palm-wine music, played at port bars for sailors and dock workers on portable instruments brought by traders. Inland it became a more African 'native blues' with 12/8 cross-rhythms.

themes.name: Brass bands and konkoma
themes.text: Local musicians in colonial military brass bands mixed marching music with local polyrhythms, creating the dance styles adaha and, on cheaper instruments, konkoma.

themes.name: Music of the high life
themes.text: In the 1920s dance orchestras played orchestrated local songs at exclusive clubs; people outside, who could not afford the fee and evening dress, called it 'the highlife'. In 1928 Jacob Asare's Kumasi Trio recorded 'Yaa Amponsah', widely seen as the earliest guitar-band highlife.

themes.name: Dance bands and guitar bands
themes.text: From the 1940s highlife split into guitar bands, at first mostly rural, which E.K. Nyame's Akan Trio helped popularise, and urban dance bands like E. T. Mensah's Tempos, a band Guy Warren also played in. Warren is credited with introducing highlife to the United States.

themes.name: Igbo highlife in Nigeria
themes.text: After the Second World War highlife took hold among Nigeria's Igbo people, and Igbo highlife became Nigeria's most popular music in the 1960s. Rex Lawson's Majors Band and Victor Uwaifo, whose 'Joromi' won Africa's first gold disc, were leading names.

schools.name: Afrobeats
schools.description: Afrobeats is less a single style than an umbrella name for the pop music flowing out of Nigeria and Ghana and their diaspora, gathering hiplife, highlife, jùjú, azonto and more. It took shape in the 2000s and 2010s in Lagos, Accra and London, where the name was coined to make the mix easier for British listeners to find. Since the late 2010s it has won wide global attention: its Spotify streams grew 550% between 2017 and 2022.
schools.debatable: The label itself is argued over: Fela Kuti's children and several artists, Burna Boy among them, prefer 'Afropop', 'Afro-fusion' or 'Nigerian pop', and some call 'afrobeats' a marketing category that hides local styles.
schools.tagline: Today's West African pop umbrella; not Fela Kuti's 1960s–70s Afrobeat, which has no 's'.
questions: A driving drum pattern that leads the song, often a 3–2 or 2–3 rhythm called a clave over a normal 4/4 beat, echoing traditional West African drums.
A tempo and momentum close to house music, though the average has slowed from about 119 to 114 beats per minute in the last decade.
Nigerian or Ghanaian accented English mixed with pidgin, slang and local languages such as Yoruba.

themes.name: Not Afrobeat
themes.text: Afrobeat is Fela Kuti's 1960s–70s style of big bands, long solos and jazzy rhythms, often political. Afrobeats takes some influence from it but is a looser blend of many West African and diaspora sounds, and usually steers clear of politics. Burna Boy and Wizkid have both sampled Fela.

themes.name: Named in London
themes.text: London DJ Abrantee is credited with adding the 's' to package the sound for British dance floors. His Choice FM show from 2011 and DJ Edu's on BBC Radio 1Xtra gave African records a UK platform, and in 2020 the UK's Official Charts Company announced an official afrobeats chart.

themes.name: Dance crazes
themes.text: Dances helped the music travel. Fuse ODG brought Ghana's Azonto to London, and Davido promoted 'Skelewu' with an instructional video that fans copied in their own uploads.

themes.name: 'One Dance' and after
themes.text: Drake's 2016 'One Dance' with Wizkid and Kyla became Spotify's most streamed song and is credited with pushing afrobeats into the worldwide mainstream. Wizkid then signed a record deal with RCA, and big labels began investing in afrobeats artists.

themes.name: An R&B-infused 2020s sound
themes.text: In the early 2020s new artists such as Tems, Rema and Ayra Starr brought an R&B-infused, sometimes trap-tinged sound. 'Essence' by Wizkid and Tems reached the US top ten, and women such as Tems and Ayra Starr broke streaming records.

schools.name: Amapiano (with kwaito)
schools.description: Amapiano is South African house music built on piano melodies, deep house, soul and jazz, and a wide, percussive 'log drum' bassline. It grew in the Gauteng townships in the mid-2010s and became popular across Africa and beyond in the early 2020s. Its roots go back to kwaito, the slow township house music that emerged in Soweto around the end of apartheid.
schools.debatable: Amapiano has no single founder: some place its start in Pretoria because it resembles bacardi house, others in the Johannesburg townships, and the electronic log drum is older than amapiano, possibly first developed by the kwaito pioneer M'du.
schools.tagline: Piano-led South African house hybrid with a wide, percussive log-drum bass; kwaito-rooted.
questions: The log drum: a deep, wide, percussive bass sound, an electronic take on the West African log drum.
Piano melodies over deep-house grooves ('amapiano' comes from the isiZulu word for 'pianos').
Vocals in many of South Africa's languages, from isiZulu and Sesotho to English and Afrikaans.

themes.name: Kwaito: slow township house
themes.text: Kwaito emerged in Soweto in the late 1980s and 1990s: house slowed down, with deep synth bass, catchy loops and samples of South African music, hip-hop and disco. It needed no formal training or costly instruments, so young people in under-funded townships could make it.

themes.name: Music of new freedom
themes.text: Kwaito is called the sound of the generation that came of age after apartheid, and anti-apartheid chants turned up in its lyrics. Arthur Mafokate's 'Kaffir' spoke about the freedoms that followed 1994.

themes.name: Women in a male scene
themes.text: Kwaito was largely run by men, and its lyrics often objectified women. Brenda Fassie took up the style in the 1990s, and the group Boom Shaka became a voice for young women.

themes.name: The log drum arrives
themes.text: Amapiano blends kwaito, deep house, gqom, jazz and soul, and made the log drum, a wide percussive bassline, one of its most popular elements. Kabza de Small credits a producer he calls MDU with figuring out the log-drum sound, though the electronic log drum may be older than amapiano.

themes.name: Pianos go global
themes.text: Amapiano spread across Africa from 2019, got its own awards in 2021 and its own Beatport charts in 2022. Tyla's 'Water', a blend with afrobeats, went viral in 2023 and charted around the world.

schools.name: Hi-NRG (with Italo disco)
schools.description: Hi-NRG ('high energy') is uptempo disco or electronic dance music, with a fast beat, pumping octave basslines and big, dramatic vocals. It grew out of late-1970s disco and became mainstream in the US gay club scene in the early 1980s before crossing into the UK charts. Italo disco, which grew in Italy from post-disco, synth-pop and hi-NRG itself, was usually sung in English.
schools.debatable: Listeners disagree whether hi-NRG is more rock than disco and whether it lacks funk, and the word was used both for any fast disco and for one narrower 1980s style; Italo disco's name is tied to the German label ZYX's marketing, but it is unclear whether ZYX actually coined it.
schools.tagline: Fast, camp disco built on pulsing octave basslines, a gay club sound of the early 1980s.
questions: An octave-jumping synth bassline, often in fast repeating sixteenth notes, as in Donna Summer's 'I Feel Love'.
A four-on-the-floor kick (a bass drum on every beat), staccato hi-hats and loud claps at 120–140 beats per minute.
Big, reverb-soaked vocals and lyrics that are often camp, tongue-in-cheek and full of double meanings.

themes.name: 'I Feel Love' starts it
themes.text: Donna Summer said 'I Feel Love' (1977) was a hit because of its 'high-energy vibe', and the phrase stuck to fast electronic disco; it is called the first hi-NRG song. Patrick Cowley's long remix of it became a collector's item.

themes.name: Gay club soundtrack
themes.text: In the early 1980s hi-NRG became mainstream in the US gay community. One theatrical strand, with diva personas and drag performers such as Sylvester and Divine, had a large cult following among San Francisco's Black and white gay men. Cowley's 'Menergy' was a frank celebration of the gay club scene.

themes.name: Slamming, not swinging
themes.text: London DJ Ian Levine defined hi-NRG as melodic, straightforward dance music that is not too funky. Producers such as Bobby Orlando built it from dense synths, rolling bass and cowbells.

themes.name: British chart era
themes.text: A UK hi-NRG chart began in 1983, and Hazell Dean's 'Searchin'' crossed into the pop charts. Stock Aitken Waterman then took the sound to number one with Dead or Alive and Bananarama.

sources.section: Formation and early hits: Divine, Hazell Dean, Dead or Alive (1984–1985)

themes.name: Italo disco
themes.text: In Italy, post-disco and synth-pop turned into Italo disco: drum machines, catchy melodies, vocoders and accented English lyrics about love, robots and space. Only a few Italo disco singles reached the UK charts, among them Sabrina's 'Boys', a top-five hit.

schools.name: Industrial (with EBM)
schools.description: Industrial music is experimental music that emerged in the mid-to-late 1970s, inspired by industrial society and built from tape loops, noise, sound collage and early electronics. The term was coined in 1976 by Monte Cazazza and adopted by Throbbing Gristle, whose confrontational style shaped the scene; after they split in 1981 it branched into many 'post-industrial' styles, among them electronic body music (EBM), which put industrial sounds on a danceable beat. By the 1990s acts such as Nine Inch Nails had brought its sounds to the mainstream.
schools.debatable: By the 1990s the label had stretched so far that journalist James Greer called it 'the kind of meaningless catch-all term that new wave once was', and Trent Reznor of Nine Inch Nails, the act described as largely responsible for bringing industrial to a mass audience, has never referred to his own work as industrial.
schools.tagline: Noise and tape-loop music about machine-age society, later made danceable as EBM.
questions: Tape edits, distorted loops, stark percussion and treated vocals, often from homemade instruments.
In EBM, a programmed four-on-the-floor or rock beat (a kick on every beat, or kick and snare) under repetitive sequenced basslines.
In EBM, samples of hammer blows, machines and alarms create a 'factory ambiance', alongside clips of political speeches and science-fiction films.

themes.name: Industrial Music for Industrial People
themes.text: The phrase was coined in 1976 by Monte Cazazza and became the slogan of Throbbing Gristle's label, Industrial Records. The first wave was Throbbing Gristle, Cabaret Voltaire from Sheffield and Boyd Rice in the US, and their work spread into mail art, performance and installations.

themes.name: Anti-music
themes.text: Throbbing Gristle rejected rock's structures and called industrial 'anti-music'. Shows could be deliberately provocative, using taboo imagery and even turning bright lights on the audience.

themes.name: Metal on metal
themes.text: In Germany, Einstürzende Neubauten played metal percussion, jackhammers and bones, and groups like Test Dept made music from metal crashing against metal.

themes.name: Body music
themes.text: In the early 1980s German and Belgian acts such as DAF and Front 242 blended industrial sounds and electronic punk with danceable rhythms and repeating sequencer lines (short note patterns played automatically by a machine). Front 242 called it electronic body music, a phrase Kraftwerk had used years before.

themes.name: Into the mainstream
themes.text: Chicago's Wax Trax! label spread the post-industrial sound, and in the 1990s industrial found a big audience among suburban and rural youth. Nine Inch Nails had several platinum records, including The Downward Spiral.

schools.name: Hardcore (techno)
schools.description: Hardcore, or hardcore techno, is electronic dance music at 160 to 200 beats per minute or faster, built on a distorted, buzzing ('sawtooth') kick drum. It grew in Belgium, the Netherlands and Germany at the turn of the 1990s, from industrial music, EBM, new beat and acid house, and in Rotterdam it became gabber. The scene grew fast again at the end of the 2010s, when Thunderdome 2019 drew almost 40,000 people.
schools.debatable: 'Hardcore' has meant many things: harder punk, harder hip-hop, and in early-1990s England a fast breakbeat rave sound that led to jungle, quite separate from the continental hardcore techno described here.
schools.tagline: Techno pushed to 160–200 bpm with a distorted kick, from Rotterdam, Frankfurt and Belgium.
questions: A distorted, buzzing kick drum, pushed hard with saturation (deliberate overdriving), and intense synthesized bass.
Very fast tempos, from 160–180 beats per minute in older styles to 200 and beyond since about 2015.
Sharp synth 'stabs' (short, punchy synth hits), such as the 'Mentasm' sound popularised by Belgian producers, and aggressive vocals.

themes.name: Industrial roots
themes.text: Hardcore is rooted in 1970s and early-1980s industrial music by groups such as Throbbing Gristle and Cabaret Voltaire. In the 1980s Belgium's EBM, hardened by new beat and acid house, set the stage, and the genre's beginnings are traced to the late-1980s Belgian new beat scene.

themes.name: Frankfurt's first track
themes.text: Marc Trauner's 'We Have Arrived' (1990), as Mescalinum United, is often regarded as the first hardcore techno track. Belgian producers of the early 1990s popularised the synth stabs that became part of the sound.

themes.name: Rotterdam gabber
themes.text: In Rotterdam, Paul Elstak and Rob Fabrie popularised a speedier style with saturated basslines, soon called gabber, and its happier, more commercial form, happy hardcore. From 1993 ID&T's Thunderdome compilations and parties drew thousands of young people into the gabber movement.

themes.name: Across borders
themes.text: In 1991 New York DJ Lenny Dee launched Industrial Strength Records, the first dedicated hardcore label, and its first release was 'We Have Arrived'. In France, Liza 'N' Eliaz and Laurent Hô pioneered a scene that later became frenchcore.

themes.name: Faster still
themes.text: In the early 2010s hardcore grew internationally, with artists such as Angerfist gaining popularity quickly. Around 2015 the scene shifted towards faster frenchcore and uptempo styles above 200 beats per minute, and Thunderdome 2019 drew almost 40,000 people.

schools.name: Grime
schools.description: Grime is electronic dance music that emerged in East London in the early 2000s, growing out of UK garage with influences from jungle, dancehall and hip-hop. Its fast, choppy beats around 140 beats per minute and cold, jagged electronic sounds leave space for MCs, whose lyrics often paint gritty pictures of city life. It grew on pirate radio and DVDs, broke through with Dizzee Rascal in 2003, faded, then returned to the charts in the mid-2010s.
schools.debatable: Nobody agrees on the first grime record: Pay As U Go's 'Know We', So Solid Crew's 'Dilemma', Wiley's 'Eskimo' and Dizzee Rascal's 'Crime' are all named, and grime is often compared with hip hop though usually held to be distinct.
schools.tagline: East London MC (rapper) music: UK garage made dark and jagged, about 140 beats a minute.
questions: Choppy, syncopated beats at around 140 beats per minute, built in 8- or 16-bar cycles; in the early '8-bar' style the beat switches every eight bars.
Cold, futuristic synths and deep, guttural sub-bass, sometimes with video-game-style sounds.
An MC up front over the beat, and clashes between MCs, generally considered an important part of grime culture.

themes.name: From dark garage
themes.text: In the late 1990s a darker, more instrumental strand of UK garage left space for MCs. Wiley called his cold, sparse version 'eskibeat', and journalists later called the gritty, bass-heavy sound 'grime'.

themes.name: Pirate radio and DVDs
themes.text: Grime spread through pirate stations such as Rinse FM, then through DVD series like Lord of the Mics, the TV channel Channel U and phones sharing tracks by Bluetooth. Clashes between MCs became central to the culture.

sources.section: 2004–2007: Treddin' on Thin Ice, Da 2nd Phaze and Playtime Is Over

themes.name: Youth making music for youth
themes.text: Many MCs were teenagers: Dizzee Rascal had his first hit at 16, and his Boy in da Corner won the 2003 Mercury Prize. Lady Sovereign was signed to Def Jam by Jay-Z and appeared on the Late Show with David Letterman.

themes.name: Decline and comeback
themes.text: By the late 2000s grime struggled for exposure and many MCs turned to pop, while online platforms such as SB.TV and GRM Daily gave artists an outlet without traditional media. In 2014 an MC-led revival began, with Skepta's 'That's Not Me' among the hits.

themes.name: Number one
themes.text: Skepta's Konnichiwa won the 2016 Mercury Prize, and Stormzy's Gang Signs & Prayer became the first grime album to top the UK chart in 2017. In 2019 Stormzy headlined Glastonbury.
